questions.stem: An investigator studies signaling in gastric parietal cells. Activation of one receptor produces the strongest acid secretory response by coupling to Gs, increasing intracellular cAMP, and activating protein kinase A to drive the H+/K+-ATPase. Which of the following mediators acts through this receptor?

explanation.summary: Histamine acting on parietal-cell H2 receptors is the strongest stimulus for gastric acid secretion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Histamine binds the H2 receptor coupled to the Gs pathway, raising cAMP and activating protein kinase A, which stimulates the H+/K+-ATPase. The brick states histamine produces the strongest acid secretory response of the three major stimuli.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acetylcholine acts on M3 receptors through the Gq pathway to raise calcium, not cAMP.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gastrin acts through the Gq pathway and also stimulates ECL cells to release histamine; it does not use Gs/cAMP directly.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Somatostatin acts through the Gi pathway to lower cAMP and inhibits acid secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prostaglandins act through the Gi pathway to decrease cAMP and inhibit acid secretion.

questions.topicName: Acid Suppression Drugs: PPIs and H2 Receptor Antagonists

questions.stem: A 56-year-old woman with long-standing gastroesophageal reflux disease is started on omeprazole. Which of the following best describes the mechanism by which this drug suppresses gastric acid?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reversibly blocks histamine H2 receptors on parietal cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Irreversibly inactivates the parietal cell H+/K+-ATPase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Chemically neutralizes acid already present in the stomach

choices.label: D
choices.text: Blocks M3 muscarinic receptors on parietal cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prevents release of gastrin from antral G cells

explanation.summary: PPIs irreversibly inactivate the parietal cell H+/K+-ATPase (proton pump).
explanation.whyCorrect: Omeprazole is a lipophilic weak base that irreversibly inactivates the H+/K+-ATPase, the transporter responsible for producing stomach acid. Because it blocks the final common pathway for H+ secretion, it inhibits acid release in response to all three stimuli (acetylcholine, histamine, and gastrin), giving a potent, long-lasting effect.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This describes H2 receptor antagonists such as famotidine, not PPIs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neutralizing existing acid describes antacids, not PPIs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PPIs do not block muscarinic receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PPIs act at the proton pump, not on gastrin release.

questions.topicName: Acid Suppression Drugs: PPIs and H2 Receptor Antagonists

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man uses over-the-counter famotidine for reflux symptoms that are worst at night. Which of the following best describes how this medication reduces gastric acid?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reversibly blocks histamine H2 receptors on parietal cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Irreversibly inactivates the H+/K+-ATPase in parietal cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Stimulates somatostatin receptors on parietal cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inhibits release of gastrin-releasing peptide from vagal fibers

choices.label: E
choices.text: Blocks M3 muscarinic receptors to reduce calcium signaling

explanation.summary: H2 receptor antagonists reversibly block parietal-cell histamine H2 receptors, especially reducing nocturnal acid secretion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Famotidine is an H2 blocker that reversibly blocks histamine H2 receptors on parietal cells, inhibiting H+ production. It is particularly effective against nocturnal acid secretion, which is largely mediated by histamine.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Irreversible inactivation of the H+/K+-ATPase is the mechanism of PPIs, not H2 blockers.
whyWrongByChoice.C: H2 blockers antagonize histamine receptors; they do not stimulate somatostatin receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: H2 blockers do not act on vagal gastrin-releasing peptide signaling.
whyWrongByChoice.E: H2 blockers do not block muscarinic M3 receptors.

questions.topicName: Acid Suppression Drugs: PPIs and H2 Receptor Antagonists

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man treated for peptic ulcer disease with long-term cimetidine develops bilateral gynecomastia and decreased libido. Which property of cimetidine best explains these findings?

explanation.summary: Cimetidine's anti-androgenic effects can cause gynecomastia and impotence.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick identifies cimetidine as an exception among H2 blockers, noting that it has anti-androgenic effects that can result in gynecomastia and impotence. Newer H2 blockers such as famotidine lack this effect and are preferred.

whyWrongByChoice.B: CYP inhibition by cimetidine causes drug interactions and toxic levels of other drugs, not gynecomastia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cimetidine is an H2 blocker and does not inactivate the proton pump.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased gastric pH and malabsorption are long-term PPI effects, not the cause of gynecomastia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reversible H2 blockade is the therapeutic mechanism and does not by itself explain the endocrine effects.

questions.topicName: Acid Suppression Drugs: PPIs and H2 Receptor Antagonists

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman who is 12 weeks pregnant has persistent heartburn and asks for a histamine H2 blocker. Which of the following medications is most appropriate to avoid because it crosses the blood-brain barrier and placenta?

explanation.summary: Cimetidine crosses the blood-brain barrier and placenta and should not be used during pregnancy.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states cimetidine crosses the blood-brain barrier and placenta, so it should not be used during pregnancy; a newer H2 blocker such as famotidine should be used instead.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Famotidine is a newer H2 blocker with fewer adverse effects and is the preferred alternative.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Omeprazole is a PPI and is not the H2 blocker singled out as unsafe in pregnancy here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pantoprazole is a PPI, not the drug specifically flagged as crossing the placenta.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ranitidine is another H2 blocker but is not the one the brick identifies as unsafe in pregnancy.

questions.topicName: Acid Suppression Drugs: PPIs and H2 Receptor Antagonists

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman who has taken omeprazole daily for 9 years sustains a low-trauma hip fracture, and bone densitometry shows osteoporosis. Which mechanism of chronic PPI use best explains this complication?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Direct inhibition of osteoblast H2 receptors

choices.label: C
choices.text: Excess renal calcium excretion from tubular injury

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased vitamin D catabolism by CYP enzymes

explanation.summary: Chronic PPI use raises gastric pH, decreasing calcium absorption and increasing fracture and osteoporosis risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: By raising gastric pH (making it less acidic), long-term PPIs decrease absorption of Ca2+, Mg2+, and Fe2+ in the GI tract. Reduced calcium absorption increases the risk of osteoporosis and fractures, which is particularly important in elderly patients.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The mechanism is malabsorption from higher gastric pH, not direct action on bone H2 receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The brick attributes fracture risk to decreased GI calcium absorption, not renal wasting.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PPI-related fracture risk is due to malabsorption, not vitamin D catabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PPIs are not described as suppressing parathyroid hormone.

questions.topicName: Acid Suppression Drugs: PPIs and H2 Receptor Antagonists

questions.stem: An 80-year-old nursing-home resident who has taken a proton pump inhibitor for several years develops profuse diarrhea and is diagnosed with Clostridioides difficile colitis. Which effect of long-term PPI therapy best explains this susceptibility?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reduced gastric acidity altering gut flora

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inhibition of intestinal H+/K+-ATPase in colonocytes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased gastric acid promoting bacterial spore germination

explanation.summary: Long-term PPI use raises gastric pH and alters gut microbiota, increasing risk of C. difficile infection and pneumonia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that patients on extended PPI therapy have an increased risk of infection such as C. difficile and pneumonia, because altered gastric pH lets normal flora become opportunistic pathogens and changes the gut microbiota.

whyWrongByChoice.B: PPIs are not described as directly immunosuppressing intestinal lymphocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Anti-androgenic effects belong to cimetidine and are unrelated to C. difficile infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PPIs act on gastric parietal cells; they do not target a colonic proton pump to cause infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PPIs decrease, not increase, gastric acid; the increased infection risk comes from higher pH.

questions.topicName: Acid Suppression Drugs: PPIs and H2 Receptor Antagonists

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man on chronic omeprazole is found to have a macrocytic anemia. Laboratory studies confirm vitamin B12 deficiency. Which mechanism of long-term PPI use best accounts for this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increased gastric pH reducing vitamin B12 absorption

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Accelerated hepatic metabolism of vitamin B12

choices.label: D
choices.text: Bone marrow suppression from proton pump blockade

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased renal excretion of vitamin B12

explanation.summary: By raising gastric pH, long-term PPIs impair absorption of vitamin B12 (and iron), which can lead to anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists vitamin B12 deficiency among the malabsorption effects of long-term PPI use; even low-dose omeprazole can decrease B12 absorption because reduced gastric acidity impairs its uptake. Decreased iron and B12 absorption can produce anemia.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The deficiency here results from PPI-induced malabsorption, not autoimmune parietal cell destruction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PPIs do not accelerate hepatic metabolism of B12.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PPIs act at the gastric proton pump and are not described as suppressing the marrow directly.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Increased renal excretion is not the described mechanism; the problem is reduced GI absorption.

questions.topicName: Acid Suppression Drugs: PPIs and H2 Receptor Antagonists

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man stabilized on warfarin is started on cimetidine for dyspepsia. Two weeks later his INR is markedly elevated and he has gingival bleeding. Which property of cimetidine best explains this interaction?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased gastric pH reducing warfarin absorption

choices.label: C
choices.text: Induction of CYP3A4 accelerating warfarin clearance

choices.label: D
choices.text: Irreversible inhibition of the proton pump

choices.label: E
choices.text: Displacement of vitamin K from hepatic stores

explanation.summary: Cimetidine inhibits multiple CYP enzymes, raising other drugs to supratherapeutic or toxic levels.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states cimetidine inhibits CYP3A4, 1A2, 2C19, and 2D6, so it can cause supratherapeutic or even toxic levels of other medications. Reduced metabolism of warfarin raises its levels and the INR, increasing bleeding risk.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Elevated INR reflects reduced warfarin metabolism from CYP inhibition, not decreased absorption.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cimetidine inhibits rather than induces CYP enzymes, so it would not accelerate clearance.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cimetidine is an H2 blocker and does not inhibit the proton pump.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cimetidine does not displace vitamin K from hepatic stores.

questions.topicName: Acid Suppression Drugs: PPIs and H2 Receptor Antagonists

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman with severe erosive esophagitis has had inadequate relief on an over-the-counter H2 blocker, and her physician wants the most potent acid suppression available. Which class of medication provides the greatest acid suppression?

explanation.summary: PPIs provide more potent acid suppression than H2 blockers because they block the final common pathway for acid secretion.
explanation.whyCorrect: PPIs irreversibly inactivate the proton pump and inhibit acid secretion in response to all three stimuli, making them more potent than H2RAs. When higher amounts of acid suppression are needed, PPIs are preferred and are first line for indications such as erosive GERD.

whyWrongByChoice.B: H2 blockers only inhibit histamine-driven acid production, making them less potent than PPIs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antacids neutralize existing acid but do not reduce acid production and are not the most potent option.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Muscarinic antagonists are not the acid-suppression drugs discussed for this indication.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prostaglandin analogs are not the class used for maximal acid suppression here.

questions.topicName: Acid Suppression Drugs: PPIs and H2 Receptor Antagonists

questions.stem: In the control of gastric acid secretion, postganglionic fibers of the vagus nerve release a peptide that stimulates antral G cells to secrete gastrin. Which of the following is this peptide?

explanation.summary: Vagal postganglionic fibers release gastrin-releasing peptide (GRP), which stimulates G cells to secrete gastrin.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that postganglionic fibers of the vagus nerve release gastrin-releasing peptide, which binds to G cells; the G cells then release gastrin, which acts on parietal and ECL cells to promote acid secretion.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Histamine is released from ECL cells, not from vagal fibers to stimulate G cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Somatostatin inhibits acid secretion; it does not stimulate G cells to release gastrin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Acetylcholine acts on parietal cell M3 receptors; the vagal peptide that triggers gastrin release is GRP.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Secretin is not described in the brick as the peptide stimulating gastrin release.

questions.topicName: Acid Suppression Drugs: PPIs and H2 Receptor Antagonists

questions.stem: A hospitalized patient who is kept nil per os after abdominal surgery requires intravenous acid suppression, and the team wants a proton pump inhibitor. Which PPI is the only one available both intravenously and orally, making it the common inpatient choice?

explanation.summary: Pantoprazole is the only PPI available intravenously and orally, making it the popular inpatient choice.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that pantoprazole is the only PPI available intravenously and orally, so it is the most popular choice in the inpatient setting.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Omeprazole is available by prescription and over the counter but is not described as the IV inpatient option.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Rabeprazole is an oral PPI and is not the intravenous inpatient choice noted here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lansoprazole is an oral PPI and is not the drug identified as available IV.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cimetidine is an H2 blocker, not a PPI.

questions.topicName: Acid Suppression Drugs: PPIs and H2 Receptor Antagonists

questions.stem: A pharmacology student studies how vagal stimulation drives gastric acid secretion. Acetylcholine released onto parietal cells binds a receptor whose activation ultimately activates the H+/K+-ATPase. Which of the following best describes the receptor and second-messenger pathway involved?

choices.label: A
choices.text: M3 receptor coupled to Gq with increased intracellular Ca2+

choices.label: B
choices.text: H2 receptor coupled to Gs with increased cAMP

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gastrin receptor coupled to Gi with decreased cAMP

choices.label: D
choices.text: M3 receptor coupled to Gs with increased cAMP

choices.label: E
choices.text: Somatostatin receptor coupled to Gq with increased Ca2+

explanation.summary: Acetylcholine binds parietal-cell M3 receptors, activating the Gq pathway and raising Ca2+ to drive the proton pump.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that acetylcholine binds M3 receptors on parietal cells, which activates the Gq pathway, increases intracellular Ca2+, and activates the H+/K+-ATPase to release H+.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The H2 receptor/Gs/cAMP pathway is the histamine pathway, not the acetylcholine pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The gastrin receptor signals through Gq, not Gi, and gastrin is not the ligand released by vagal fibers onto parietal cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: M3 receptors couple to Gq and Ca2+, not to Gs and cAMP.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Somatostatin receptors couple to Gi and decrease cAMP; they inhibit rather than stimulate acid secretion.

questions.topicName: Acid Suppression Drugs: PPIs and H2 Receptor Antagonists

questions.stem: An investigator applies two endogenous mediators to isolated parietal cells and observes that both reduce H+ secretion by lowering intracellular cAMP. Which pair of mediators and G-protein pathway best explains this observation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Histamine and gastrin acting through Gs

choices.label: B
choices.text: Acetylcholine and gastrin acting through Gq

choices.label: C
choices.text: Somatostatin and prostaglandins acting through Gi

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gastrin-releasing peptide and histamine acting through Gi

choices.label: E
choices.text: Somatostatin and acetylcholine acting through Gs

explanation.summary: Somatostatin and prostaglandins inhibit acid secretion via Gi-coupled receptors that decrease cAMP.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that somatostatin and prostaglandins inhibit acid secretion by acting on their receptors, resulting in activation of the Gi pathway and a decrease in cAMP within parietal cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Histamine uses Gs to raise cAMP and stimulate acid; gastrin uses Gq. Neither lowers cAMP.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Acetylcholine and gastrin both act through Gq and raise Ca2+ to stimulate, not inhibit, acid secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gastrin-releasing peptide acts on G cells, and histamine stimulates acid via Gs; neither is a Gi-coupled inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Acetylcholine stimulates acid via Gq, and somatostatin acts through Gi rather than Gs.

questions.topicName: Acid Suppression Drugs: PPIs and H2 Receptor Antagonists

questions.stem: A researcher measures histamine release from enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells in the gastric mucosa after exposing them to a circulating hormone. Histamine release rises sharply, and nearby parietal cells then increase H+ secretion. Which hormone most likely triggered the ECL cell response?

explanation.summary: Gastrin binds receptors on ECL cells, stimulating histamine release that then acts on parietal-cell H2 receptors.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that gastrin binds the gastrin receptor on both parietal cells and ECL cells; in ECL cells this leads to secretion of histamine, which binds H2 receptors on nearby parietal cells and produces the strongest acid secretory response.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Secretin is released from duodenal S cells and is not described as stimulating ECL cell histamine release.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cholecystokinin is released from duodenal I cells and is not the stimulus for ECL histamine release.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Somatostatin inhibits acid secretion; it would not increase histamine-driven H+ secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Gastric inhibitory peptide from K cells is not the hormone that drives ECL histamine release.

questions.topicName: Acid Suppression Drugs: PPIs and H2 Receptor Antagonists

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man eats a large protein-rich meal. Within minutes, his gastric acid output rises, and serum gastrin levels increase. Which of the following best describes two non-neural stimuli that promote gastrin release from antral G cells in this setting?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Low gastric pH and bile acid reflux

choices.label: B
choices.text: Stomach distention and partially digested proteins

choices.label: D
choices.text: Histamine from ECL cells and somatostatin from D cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Elevated cAMP in parietal cells and mucus secretion

explanation.summary: Beyond vagal gastrin-releasing peptide, gastrin is released by stomach distention and the presence of partially digested proteins.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that gastrin is released in response to gastrin-releasing peptide from vagal fibers, and is also released by distention of the stomach and the presence of partially digested proteins. Gastrin then acts on parietal and ECL cells to promote acid secretion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Low gastric pH and bile reflux are not described as stimuli for gastrin release.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Duodenal fat and secretin are duodenal signals and are not identified as G-cell stimulants.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Histamine acts downstream on parietal cells, and somatostatin inhibits acid secretion; neither is described as triggering gastrin release.
whyWrongByChoice.E: cAMP elevation and mucus secretion are not stimuli acting on G cells.

questions.topicName: Acid Suppression Drugs: PPIs and H2 Receptor Antagonists

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with gastroesophageal reflux disease has persistent symptoms despite daily omeprazole taken correctly. Her physician wants to add a second acid-suppressing agent as an adjunct rather than replace the PPI. Which of the following is the most appropriate addition?

explanation.summary: H2 blockers may be used as an adjunct in patients with a poor response to PPIs.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that H2 blockers are effective in GERD, peptic ulcer disease, and gastritis and may be used as adjunct therapy in patients with a poor response to PPIs. Famotidine is the newer H2 blocker preferred over cimetidine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pantoprazole is another PPI, which would duplicate the mechanism the patient is already using rather than add an adjunct.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Esomeprazole is a PPI; adding a second PPI does not provide the adjunctive H2-blocking mechanism described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rabeprazole is a PPI, not an adjunct of a different class.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lansoprazole is a PPI and would not serve as the adjunct class described.

questions.topicName: Acid Suppression Drugs: PPIs and H2 Receptor Antagonists

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman brings in a bottle of esomeprazole she purchased for heartburn and asks how it works. Based on its name, this drug most likely belongs to which of the following classes?

explanation.summary: The -prazole suffix identifies proton pump inhibitors; the -dine suffix identifies H2 blockers.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists omeprazole, lansoprazole, esomeprazole, pantoprazole, and rabeprazole as commonly used PPIs and highlights the -prazole suffix. It also notes that omeprazole and esomeprazole are available both by prescription and over the counter.

whyWrongByChoice.A: H2 receptor antagonists carry the -dine suffix (cimetidine, famotidine, ranitidine).
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antacids neutralize existing acid and are not named with the -prazole suffix.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Muscarinic antagonists are not the class indicated by the -prazole suffix.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prostaglandin analogs are not identified by the -prazole suffix.

questions.topicName: Acid Suppression Drugs: PPIs and H2 Receptor Antagonists

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man is prescribed omeprazole for peptic ulcer disease. Which of the following counseling points about the timing of administration is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Take it immediately after finishing a meal

choices.label: B
choices.text: Take it 2 hours after a meal with a full glass of water

choices.label: C
choices.text: Take it only at bedtime on an empty stomach

choices.label: D
choices.text: Take it at any time; timing relative to meals does not matter

choices.label: E
choices.text: Take it at least 30 minutes before a meal

explanation.summary: PPIs should be taken at least 30 minutes before a meal.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that when a PPI is prescribed, the patient should be educated to take the drug at least 30 minutes before a meal, and that the time PPIs take to reach full effect relates to their mechanism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dosing after a meal does not follow the pre-meal timing the brick recommends.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Post-meal dosing 2 hours later is not the recommended timing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Bedtime-only dosing is not the counseling the brick gives for PPIs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Timing does matter; the brick specifically instructs pre-meal dosing.

questions.topicName: Acid Suppression Drugs: PPIs and H2 Receptor Antagonists

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with peptic ulcer disease takes famotidine. Studies of his gastric acid output show a marked reduction in nocturnal secretion but only a partial reduction in the acid surge that follows meals. Which of the following best explains the incomplete suppression of meal-stimulated acid?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Famotidine is rapidly inactivated by gastric acid after meals

choices.label: B
choices.text: Meal-stimulated acid is driven by acetylcholine and gastrin, which H2 blockers do not block

choices.label: C
choices.text: Famotidine binds the proton pump reversibly and dissociates when food arrives

choices.label: D
choices.text: Food stimulates somatostatin release, which competes with famotidine at H2 receptors

choices.label: E
choices.text: Famotidine induces its own metabolism after repeated dosing

explanation.summary: H2 blockers only inhibit histamine-mediated acid secretion, leaving acetylcholine- and gastrin-driven secretion intact.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that H2RAs significantly affect histamine-stimulated acid secretion, especially nocturnal secretion, but unlike PPIs they inhibit acid production only in response to histamine, which makes them less potent. Acid stimulated by acetylcholine and gastrin, which act through separate receptors, is not blocked.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick does not describe famotidine being inactivated by gastric acid; its limitation is receptor selectivity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Famotidine blocks H2 receptors; it does not bind the proton pump.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Somatostatin acts on its own Gi-coupled receptor and inhibits acid; it does not compete at H2 receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Autoinduction of metabolism is not a property attributed to famotidine.

questions.topicName: Acid Suppression Drugs: PPIs and H2 Receptor Antagonists

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman takes pantoprazole once daily. Her acid suppression persists well beyond the time the drug remains detectable in her plasma. Which property of PPIs best explains this prolonged effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Competitive, reversible blockade of the H2 receptor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Extensive protein binding that prolongs plasma half-life

choices.label: D
choices.text: Enterohepatic recirculation of the parent drug

choices.label: E
choices.text: Active secretion of the drug into gastric juice

explanation.summary: Irreversible inactivation of the proton pump produces a longer-lasting effect than reversible receptor blockade.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that PPIs irreversibly inactivate the parietal cell H+/K+-ATPase, and that this irreversible binding produces a longer-lasting effect and a very potent effect compared to other acid suppression therapy such as H2RAs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Reversible H2 receptor blockade is the mechanism of H2RAs and produces a shorter, less potent effect.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The brick attributes duration to irreversible pump inactivation, not to protein binding.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Enterohepatic recirculation is not described as the basis for PPI duration of action.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Secretion into gastric juice is not the mechanism given for prolonged action.

questions.topicName: Acid Suppression Drugs: PPIs and H2 Receptor Antagonists

questions.stem: A medicinal chemist describes the physicochemical properties that allow omeprazole to accumulate in the parietal cell and inactivate the proton pump. Which of the following best characterizes proton pump inhibitors as a class?

explanation.summary: PPIs are lipophilic weak bases that irreversibly inactivate the parietal cell H+/K+-ATPase.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes PPIs as lipophilic weak bases that reduce the amount of acid produced by parietal cells by irreversibly inactivating the H+/K+-ATPase, the transporter primarily responsible for producing stomach acid.

whyWrongByChoice.A: PPIs are bases, not acids, and are lipophilic rather than hydrophilic.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PPIs are not quaternary ammonium compounds.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PPIs are lipophilic, not hydrophilic.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PPIs are weak bases, not strong acids.

questions.topicName: Acid Suppression Drugs: PPIs and H2 Receptor Antagonists

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman reports occasional mild heartburn after large meals a few times per month. She has no alarm symptoms and no history of ulcers or esophagitis. Which class of medication is generally preferred as initial therapy for this presentation?

explanation.summary: For mild cases of heartburn, H2RAs are generally preferred; PPIs are reserved for when greater acid suppression is needed.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that both H2RAs and PPIs are indicated for heartburn, but for mild cases of heartburn H2RAs are generally preferred, whereas PPIs are often preferred when higher amounts of acid suppression are needed.

whyWrongByChoice.B: PPIs are preferred when higher amounts of acid suppression are needed, not for mild intermittent heartburn.
whyWrongByChoice.C: H. pylori triple therapy is for eradication of infection, not for mild heartburn without a diagnosed infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Intravenous pantoprazole is the inpatient option and is not appropriate for mild outpatient heartburn.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prostaglandin analogs are not the acid-suppressing class the brick recommends for mild heartburn.

questions.topicName: Acid Suppression Drugs: PPIs and H2 Receptor Antagonists

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man with a duodenal ulcer tests positive for Helicobacter pylori. His physician prescribes a multi-drug eradication regimen. In addition to antibiotics, which of the following acid-suppressing agents is a component of the triple therapy regimen?

explanation.summary: A PPI is a component of the triple therapy treatment plan used for H. pylori eradication.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that PPIs are first-line medical treatment for GERD, peptic ulcer disease, and gastritis, and that they are a component of the triple therapy treatment plan used for H. pylori eradication. Omeprazole is a commonly used PPI.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cimetidine is an H2 blocker and is not the class identified as part of triple therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Famotidine is an H2 blocker; the eradication regimen described uses a PPI.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ranitidine is an H2 blocker, not the PPI component of triple therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Calcium carbonate is an antacid and is not part of the H. pylori triple therapy described.

questions.topicName: Acid Suppression Drugs: PPIs and H2 Receptor Antagonists

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman is started on high-dose corticosteroids for a severe flare of an inflammatory condition. Her physician also prescribes a proton pump inhibitor even though she has no gastrointestinal symptoms. Which of the following best describes the purpose of the PPI in this setting?

explanation.summary: PPIs can be used as prophylaxis, for example during high-dose steroid therapy, and for ulcer prevention in critically ill patients.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that PPIs can be used as treatment or prophylaxis, giving high-dose steroid use as an example, and lists prevention of ulcers in critically ill patients among the shared indications of H2RAs and PPIs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: PPIs are not given to improve steroid absorption; if anything, raised gastric pH alters absorption of other drugs.
whyWrongByChoice.B: H. pylori eradication requires a triple therapy regimen and is not the purpose here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hypomagnesemia is an adverse effect of long-term PPI use, not something PPIs prevent.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The patient has no symptoms or diagnosed esophagitis; the PPI is preventive, not treatment.

questions.topicName: Acid Suppression Drugs: PPIs and H2 Receptor Antagonists

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man started omeprazole 1 week ago for gastritis. He reports a new mild headache and loose stools but is otherwise well. Which of the following best characterizes these symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Signs of hypomagnesemia requiring urgent electrolyte replacement

choices.label: B
choices.text: Early manifestations of Clostridium difficile colitis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Anti-androgenic effects requiring a drug switch

choices.label: D
choices.text: Common short-term adverse effects of PPIs

explanation.summary: Short-term PPI use is generally safe; the most common side effects are headache, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that PPIs are generally safe and well tolerated when used short term, and that the most common short-term side effects include headache, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Long-term use is what raises risk for the more serious adverse effects.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hypomagnesemia is a long-term malabsorption effect and is not suggested by mild headache and loose stools after 1 week.
whyWrongByChoice.B: C. difficile infection is a long-term risk of extended PPI use, not the expected explanation for mild symptoms after 1 week.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Anti-androgenic effects belong to cimetidine, not to PPIs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin B12 malabsorption develops with long-term use and does not present as headache and loose stools.

questions.topicName: Acid Suppression Drugs: PPIs and H2 Receptor Antagonists

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with a history of heart failure and prior atrial fibrillation has taken omeprazole for 6 years. He presents with palpitations, and an ECG shows a new arrhythmia. Serum electrolytes reveal a low level of a divalent cation. Which of the following is the most likely electrolyte abnormality related to his medication?

explanation.summary: Long-term PPI use can cause hypomagnesemia, which is troublesome in patients with cardiac comorbidities because it increases arrhythmia risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that by raising gastric pH, PPIs decrease absorption of Ca2+, Mg2+, and Fe2+ over time, and that this can lead to hypomagnesemia, which could be troublesome for patients with a history of cardiac comorbidities and can increase their risk for arrhythmias.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Potassium is not a divalent cation, and hyperkalemia is not a described PPI effect.
whyWrongByChoice.B: PPIs decrease calcium absorption; they would lower, not raise, calcium.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sodium is monovalent, and hyponatremia is not a described PPI complication.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PPIs cause magnesium deficiency through malabsorption, not magnesium excess.

questions.topicName: Acid Suppression Drugs: PPIs and H2 Receptor Antagonists

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman on long-term lansoprazole for GERD is found to have a microcytic, hypochromic anemia with low ferritin. She has no gastrointestinal bleeding, and her diet is adequate. Which mechanism best explains her anemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased Fe2+ absorption from elevated gastric pH

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased vitamin B12 absorption from elevated gastric pH

choices.label: E
choices.text: Chronic occult bleeding from PPI-induced ulcers

explanation.summary: Long-term PPIs raise gastric pH and reduce iron absorption, and iron malabsorption can lead to anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists Fe2+ among the ions whose absorption PPIs decrease over time because of increased gastric pH, and it states in the drug interaction section that malabsorption of vitamin B12 and iron can lead to anemia. A microcytic anemia with low ferritin points to the iron rather than the B12 pathway.

whyWrongByChoice.B: B12 malabsorption is a real PPI effect but produces a macrocytic picture, not microcytic anemia with low ferritin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CYP3A4 metabolizes PPIs and affects drug interactions; it does not destroy hemoglobin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Anti-androgenic effects belong to cimetidine and are not a cause of anemia here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PPIs treat and prevent ulcers rather than cause them, and the stem states there is no bleeding.

questions.topicName: Acid Suppression Drugs: PPIs and H2 Receptor Antagonists

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man asks his physician whether his decade-long use of a proton pump inhibitor could be affecting organs outside his gastrointestinal tract. Which of the following pairs of conditions has been associated with long-term PPI use through a mechanism that remains unclear?

explanation.summary: Long-term PPI use is correlated with chronic kidney disease and dementia, although the exact mechanism is unclear.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick groups CKD and dementia under 'Other' long-term adverse effects of PPIs, stating that long-term PPI use has been associated with an increased risk of both, that the exact mechanism is unclear, but that a correlation exists between long-term PPI use and these two disease states.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Cirrhosis and pancreatitis are not among the long-term PPI associations described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pulmonary fibrosis and glaucoma are not described as PPI-associated conditions.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gynecomastia and impotence are anti-androgenic effects of cimetidine, not PPIs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Barrett's esophagus and erosive esophagitis are complications of GERD that PPIs treat, not adverse effects of PPIs.

questions.topicName: Acid Suppression Drugs: PPIs and H2 Receptor Antagonists

questions.stem: A 42-year-old man with GERD is starting a time-limited course of acid suppression therapy. His physician recommends concurrent lifestyle and behavioral changes to see if his symptoms can be controlled without indefinite medication. Which of the following is one of the recommended changes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Eating one large meal per day

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increasing coffee intake to stimulate gastric emptying

choices.label: C
choices.text: Not eating within 3 hours of bedtime

choices.label: E
choices.text: Switching from cigarettes to smokeless tobacco

explanation.summary: Lifestyle changes for GERD include quitting smoking, reducing alcohol, eating smaller portions, and not eating within 3 hours of bedtime.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that because of the risks of long-term PPI use, patients should concurrently initiate lifestyle and behavioral changes such as quitting smoking, reducing or stopping alcohol consumption, eating smaller portions, and not eating within 3 hours of bedtime, to see if symptoms can be alleviated with time-limited acid suppression therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick recommends smaller portions, not consolidating intake into one large meal.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Increasing coffee is not among the recommended changes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lying flat after meals is not recommended; the guidance is to avoid eating close to bedtime.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The recommendation is to quit smoking, not to substitute another tobacco product.

questions.topicName: Acid Suppression Drugs: PPIs and H2 Receptor Antagonists

questions.stem: A 56-year-old woman has taken omeprazole daily for 5 years for GERD symptom control. She has no history of Barrett's esophagus, erosive esophagitis, or other GERD complications, and she is worried about long-term risks. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term management change?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increase omeprazole to twice daily for better control

choices.label: B
choices.text: Transition to famotidine as a safer long-term option

choices.label: D
choices.text: Switch to cimetidine for its broader effect profile

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stop all acid suppression and begin H. pylori triple therapy

explanation.summary: Patients on long-term PPIs without GERD complications may be better served by transitioning to an H2RA such as famotidine.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's case concludes that although PPIs provide stronger acid suppression, they may carry long-term risks such as malabsorption and infection when used indefinitely, that H2RAs can be effective for GERD and may be a safer long-term alternative, and that switching to an H2RA like famotidine or ranitidine may be a good option to avoid long-term complications.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Escalating the PPI increases exposure to the long-term risks she is concerned about and is not indicated without complications.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Intravenous pantoprazole is the inpatient formulation and is not appropriate for stable outpatient GERD.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cimetidine has a more extensive adverse effect profile; newer H2 blockers like famotidine are advised instead.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Triple therapy is for documented H. pylori infection, which is not described, and abrupt cessation of all therapy is not the recommended plan.

questions.topicName: Acid Suppression Drugs: PPIs and H2 Receptor Antagonists

questions.stem: A 39-year-old woman has heartburn, regurgitation, and difficulty swallowing. Her physician explains that her acid production is not excessive and that the problem lies elsewhere. Which of the following is the primary underlying abnormality in gastroesophageal reflux disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Overproduction of gastrin by antral G cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hypertrophy of parietal cells in the gastric body

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inappropriate weakening or relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter

choices.label: D
choices.text: Excess histamine release from ECL cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spasm of the pyloric sphincter delaying gastric emptying

explanation.summary: GERD results from a weak or inappropriately relaxing lower esophageal sphincter that lets stomach contents reflux, rather than from an acid overproduction problem.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's clinical correlation describes GERD as a chronic condition in which stomach contents reflux into the esophagus because the lower esophageal sphincter weakens or relaxes inappropriately, causing heartburn, regurgitation, and difficulty swallowing. It emphasizes that it is not so much a stomach acid problem as a weakness in the LES, and that reducing acid with PPIs or H2RAs treats the symptoms.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gastrin overproduction is not the basis of GERD described in the brick.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Parietal cell hypertrophy is not the underlying abnormality; GERD is not primarily an acid quantity problem.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Excess ECL histamine is not the cause of GERD.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pyloric sphincter spasm is not the mechanism; the defect is at the lower esophageal sphincter.

questions.topicName: Acid Suppression Drugs: PPIs and H2 Receptor Antagonists

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman has been taking famotidine for 2 weeks for heartburn. She asks which adverse effect she is most likely to experience from this medication. Which of the following is the most common side effect of famotidine?

explanation.summary: H2 blockers are generally safe; the most common side effect of famotidine is headache.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that most H2 blockers are generally safe and adverse effects are rare, and that the most common side effect of famotidine is headache.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gynecomastia is an anti-androgenic effect of cimetidine, not famotidine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Impotence is an anti-androgenic effect of cimetidine, not famotidine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Osteoporosis is a long-term PPI malabsorption effect, not a famotidine effect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hypomagnesemia is associated with long-term PPI use, not famotidine.

questions.topicName: Acid Suppression Drugs: PPIs and H2 Receptor Antagonists

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man was started on an over-the-counter H2 blocker for gastritis. Over the next month he develops diarrhea, dizziness, and a skin rash. Review of his medication reveals the specific H2 blocker he chose. Which drug most likely accounts for these findings, and what is the most appropriate change?

explanation.summary: Cimetidine has a more extensive adverse effect profile (diarrhea, dizziness, headache, rashes), so newer H2 blockers such as famotidine are preferred.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick identifies cimetidine as the exception among generally well-tolerated H2 blockers, listing diarrhea, dizziness, headache, and rashes among its adverse effects, and advises using newer H2 blockers such as famotidine instead of cimetidine because of its more extensive adverse effect profile.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Famotidine's most common side effect is headache, and switching to cimetidine would move toward the drug with the broader adverse profile.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Famotidine is not the drug implicated by this cluster of effects, and a PPI is not needed to solve a cimetidine tolerability problem.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ranitidine is not singled out for these effects, and cimetidine is the drug to avoid rather than switch to.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cimetidine is the likely culprit, but the recommended alternative is a newer oral H2 blocker like famotidine, not IV inpatient therapy.

questions.topicName: Acid Suppression Drugs: PPIs and H2 Receptor Antagonists

questions.stem: A 59-year-old woman taking a medication that is a substrate of CYP3A4 is started on omeprazole for peptic ulcer disease. Her physician is concerned about a pharmacokinetic interaction. Which of the following best explains the basis for this concern?

choices.label: A
choices.text: PPIs irreversibly inactivate CYP3A4 in hepatocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: PPIs are metabolized by CYP3A4 and can alter levels of other CYP3A4 substrates

choices.label: C
choices.text: PPIs inhibit CYP1A2, 2C19, and 2D6 but not CYP3A4

choices.label: D
choices.text: PPIs are excreted unchanged by the kidney and compete for tubular secretion

choices.label: E
choices.text: PPIs bind CYP3A4 substrates in the gut lumen and prevent their absorption

explanation.summary: PPIs are metabolized by CYP3A4, creating a myriad of potential interactions with other CYP3A4 substrates.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that PPIs are metabolized by CYP3A4, which can result in a myriad of drug interactions and altered absorption of the PPIs or the medications they interact with, and that caution should always be used when other CYP3A4 substrates are co-administered.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Irreversible inactivation is what PPIs do to the proton pump, not to CYP3A4.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inhibition of CYP3A4, 1A2, 2C19, and 2D6 describes cimetidine, and the brick's PPI concern centers on CYP3A4 metabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick attributes PPI interactions to CYP3A4 metabolism and gastric pH, not to renal tubular competition.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PPIs affect absorption of other drugs by raising gastric pH, not by binding them in the lumen.

questions.topicName: Acid Suppression Drugs: PPIs and H2 Receptor Antagonists

questions.stem: A 51-year-old woman with hypothyroidism has been well controlled on a stable dose of levothyroxine for years. Three months after starting daily omeprazole for GERD, her TSH is elevated and she reports fatigue. She takes both medications faithfully. Which of the following best explains this change?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Omeprazole induces hepatic metabolism of levothyroxine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Omeprazole stimulates TSH release from the pituitary

choices.label: C
choices.text: Omeprazole blocks thyroid hormone receptors in peripheral tissues

choices.label: D
choices.text: Omeprazole raises gastric pH and reduces levothyroxine absorption

choices.label: E
choices.text: Omeprazole displaces levothyroxine from plasma proteins

explanation.summary: Levothyroxine is one of the medications whose absorption is greatly affected by the altered gastric pH that PPIs induce.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's clinical correlation notes that other medications, giving levothyroxine for hypothyroidism as the example, are greatly affected by the altered gastric pH that PPIs induce, so drug interactions should always be considered with PPIs. Reduced absorption lowers effective thyroid hormone delivery, producing a rising TSH.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick describes PPIs as CYP3A4 substrates, not as inducers of levothyroxine metabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.B: PPIs do not act on the pituitary; the elevated TSH is secondary to reduced hormone absorption.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PPIs do not block thyroid hormone receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Protein-binding displacement is not the interaction the brick describes; the mechanism is pH-dependent absorption.

questions.topicName: Acid Suppression Drugs: PPIs and H2 Receptor Antagonists

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with seasonal allergic rhinitis takes an over-the-counter H1 antihistamine and notices that her runny nose improves. This symptom relief is most directly explained by which of the following actions of the drug on endothelial cells adjacent to vascular smooth muscle?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increased release of nitric oxide and prostacyclin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inhibition of nitric oxide and prostacyclin release

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct stimulation of mast cell degranulation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Activation of nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction

explanation.summary: H1 antihistamines reduce nasal symptoms by blocking H1 receptors, which inhibits nitric oxide and prostacyclin release and produces vasoconstriction.
explanation.whyCorrect: By antagonizing H1 receptors on endothelial cells, the drug inhibits the release of nitric oxide and prostacyclin. This causes vasoconstriction and reduces edema formation, lessening runny nose symptoms.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Increased nitric oxide and prostacyclin would cause vasodilation and worsen edema, the opposite of the drug's effect.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antihistamines block the H1 receptor; they do not trigger mast cell degranulation, which is what releases histamine in the first place.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Blocking gastric acid secretion is a function of H2 blockers, not H1 antihistamines used for allergy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: H1 antihistamines act on histamine receptors, not nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction.

questions.topicName: H1 Blockers - Antihistamines

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man takes diphenhydramine for allergies and becomes very drowsy, while his coworker taking loratadine for the same allergies reports no sedation. Which property of diphenhydramine best accounts for this difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is hydrophilic and cannot enter the brain

choices.label: B
choices.text: It selectively blocks H2 receptors in the stomach

explanation.summary: First-generation antihistamines such as diphenhydramine are lipophilic and cross the blood-brain barrier, blocking central H1 receptors and causing sedation.
explanation.whyCorrect: First-generation H1 antihistamines are lipophilic and readily cross the blood-brain barrier, so they block central H1 receptors that normally promote wakefulness, producing drowsiness. Second-generation drugs like loratadine are hydrophilic and penetrate the brain poorly, so they are non-sedating.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Diphenhydramine is lipophilic, not hydrophilic; that is precisely why it enters the brain.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Diphenhydramine blocks H1, not H2 receptors, and H2 blockade would not explain sedation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Diphenhydramine is a first-generation, not a second-generation, antihistamine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The drug blocks H1 receptors; it does not stimulate central histamine release.

questions.topicName: H1 Blockers - Antihistamines

questions.stem: A patient is prescribed a non-sedating antihistamine for chronic urticaria so that daytime alertness is preserved. Which of the following agents best fits this description?

explanation.summary: Second-generation antihistamines such as fexofenadine are non-sedating because they poorly cross the blood-brain barrier.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fexofenadine is a second-generation H1 antihistamine. These agents are hydrophilic, act primarily on peripheral H1 receptors, and cause little sedation, making them ideal when alertness must be preserved.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Diphenhydramine is a lipophilic first-generation agent that causes marked drowsiness.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Promethazine is a first-generation agent with sedating and antimuscarinic properties.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hydroxyzine is a first-generation antihistamine and is sedating.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Chlorpheniramine is a first-generation agent that crosses the blood-brain barrier and can cause sedation.

questions.topicName: H1 Blockers - Antihistamines

questions.stem: A 76-year-old man is brought in for confusion, blurred vision, dry mouth, and difficulty urinating that began after he started an over-the-counter first-generation antihistamine. These findings are best explained by the drug's action at which of the following receptors?

explanation.summary: Many first-generation antihistamines also block muscarinic receptors, producing anticholinergic side effects.
explanation.whyCorrect: First-generation H1 antihistamines have antimuscarinic (anticholinergic) activity. Blockade of muscarinic receptors causes dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, constipation, and, especially in the elderly, confusion and delirium.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Nicotinic receptor blockade would affect the neuromuscular junction and autonomic ganglia, not this pattern of anticholinergic findings.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Beta-2 blockade relates to bronchial and vascular tone, not dry mouth and urinary retention.
whyWrongByChoice.D: H2 receptors regulate gastric acid; blocking them does not cause this anticholinergic toxidrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: D2 blockade causes extrapyramidal effects, not the dry mouth, blurred vision, and urinary retention seen here.

questions.topicName: H1 Blockers - Antihistamines

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman who is 9 weeks pregnant has persistent nausea and vomiting. Her physician prescribes doxylamine in combination with which of the following, an FDA-approved regimen for nausea and vomiting of pregnancy?

explanation.summary: Doxylamine plus vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) is an approved treatment for nausea and vomiting of pregnancy.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that doxylamine, a first-generation antihistamine, combined with vitamin B6 (pyridoxine), is approved for the treatment of nausea and vomiting in pregnancy. First-generation agents cross the placenta but are unlikely to be strong risk factors for major birth defects.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Vitamin B12 is used for pernicious anemia, not paired with doxylamine for pregnancy nausea.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Folic acid prevents neural tube defects but is not the antiemetic partner of doxylamine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vitamin C is not part of this regimen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin D addresses bone and calcium metabolism, not nausea of pregnancy.

questions.topicName: H1 Blockers - Antihistamines

questions.stem: A family planning a road trip asks for a medication to prevent motion sickness in an adult. Which antihistamine is most appropriate, and what property makes it effective for this indication?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fexofenadine, because it acts only peripherally

choices.label: C
choices.text: Promethazine, because of its antimuscarinic properties

choices.label: E
choices.text: Desloratadine, because it blocks H2 receptors

explanation.summary: First-generation antihistamines with antimuscarinic activity, such as promethazine, are effective against motion sickness.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that first-generation antihistamines like promethazine and dimenhydrinate have antimuscarinic properties that make them effective in treating motion sickness. Second-generation agents lack this activity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Loratadine is a peripherally acting second-generation agent without the antimuscarinic activity needed for motion sickness.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fexofenadine acts only peripherally and is not used for motion sickness.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cetirizine is a second-generation agent lacking meaningful antimuscarinic effect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Desloratadine is an H1, not H2, agent and is second-generation; it is not used for motion sickness.

questions.topicName: H1 Blockers - Antihistamines

questions.stem: In a review of histamine physiology, a student notes where the H1 receptor is located relative to other histamine receptor subtypes. According to the brick, where are H2 histamine receptors primarily located?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Throughout the central and peripheral nervous systems

explanation.summary: H2 histamine receptors are found primarily in gastric cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that H2 histamine receptors are primarily in gastric cells, H3 receptors in the neurons, and H4 receptors in the bone marrow, whereas H1 receptors are widespread and are the target of antihistamine therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The bone marrow is the location of H4, not H2, receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The neurons are where H3 receptors are located.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Widespread distribution in the central and peripheral nervous systems describes H1 receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vascular endothelial cells express the H1 receptors targeted by antihistamines, not H2.

questions.topicName: H1 Blockers - Antihistamines

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child is given a first-generation antihistamine and, instead of becoming sleepy, develops restlessness, nervousness, and insomnia. This response is best described as which of the following?

choices.label: C
choices.text: An allergic reaction to the drug

choices.label: D
choices.text: A sign of H2 receptor blockade

choices.label: E
choices.text: A withdrawal effect from stopping the drug

explanation.summary: First-generation antihistamines can cause paradoxical CNS stimulation in children younger than about six years.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick warns that in children younger than six, first-generation antihistamines can, at regular doses, cause a paradoxical CNS stimulation manifesting as restlessness, nervousness, and insomnia rather than the usual drowsiness.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The child is stimulated, not sedated, so this is not the expected sedative effect.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The symptoms are a CNS drug effect, not an allergic (hypersensitivity) reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: These first-generation agents act at H1 and muscarinic receptors, not H2.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The reaction occurred after taking the drug, not after stopping it, so it is not withdrawal.

questions.topicName: H1 Blockers - Antihistamines

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman takes diphenhydramine for seasonal allergies. Through its anticholinergic (antimuscarinic) action, this drug is most likely to produce which of the following effects in the eye?

explanation.summary: Antimuscarinic action at the eye causes pupil dilation and reduced tear formation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Figure 2 lists the ocular anticholinergic effects as mydriasis (dilation) and decreased lacrimation, which clinically produce blurred vision and dry eyes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Miosis and increased tears are cholinergic effects, the opposite of antimuscarinic blockade.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antimuscarinic effects decrease, not increase, intestinal motility, causing constipation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antimuscarinic activity decreases sweating rather than increasing it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Antimuscarinic activity decreases urination, causing retention, not increased output.

questions.topicName: H1 Blockers - Antihistamines

questions.stem: A patient taking a second-generation antihistamine for allergies reports only a mild headache and occasional fatigue, with no significant dry mouth or drowsiness. This favorable side-effect profile compared with first-generation agents is best explained by which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Greater lipophilicity and stronger blood-brain barrier penetration

choices.label: D
choices.text: Enhanced release of histamine from mast cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Irreversible binding to H1 receptors in the brain

explanation.summary: Second-generation antihistamines penetrate the brain poorly and have little antimuscarinic activity, so side effects are mild and non-specific.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because second-generation agents are hydrophilic and act mainly on peripheral H1 receptors, they cause much less sedation and few antimuscarinic effects. Their adverse effects are usually mild and non-specific, such as headache, diarrhea, or fatigue.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Greater lipophilicity and brain penetration would increase, not decrease, sedation, and describes first-generation agents.
whyWrongByChoice.C: These drugs block H1 receptors; nicotinic blockade is not their mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antihistamines block the H1 receptor and do not enhance histamine release.
whyWrongByChoice.E: H1 antihistamines are competitive (reversible) H1 blockers, not irreversible binders.

questions.topicName: H1 Blockers - Antihistamines

questions.stem: A 78-year-old man reports several weeks of new daytime sleepiness. Medication review reveals he recently added an over-the-counter pill containing diphenhydramine to help him sleep. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to address his sleepiness?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add a second-generation antihistamine on top of the diphenhydramine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Switch to promethazine for its antimuscarinic effect

choices.label: E
choices.text: Add an H2 blocker to counteract the sedation

explanation.summary: Sedation from a first-generation antihistamine is managed by stopping the offending drug and substituting a non-sedating agent if needed.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the case, the patient's new sleepiness is caused by diphenhydramine, a sedating first-generation antihistamine. The remedy is to stop that drug and, if antihistamine therapy is still needed, replace it with a non-sedating second-generation agent such as loratadine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adding another antihistamine keeps the sedating diphenhydramine on board and does not fix the problem.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Increasing the dose of the sedating drug would worsen the sleepiness.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Promethazine is another sedating first-generation agent and would not relieve the drowsiness.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An H2 blocker treats gastric acid and would not counteract the sedation from an H1 agent.

questions.topicName: H1 Blockers - Antihistamines

questions.stem: H1 antihistamines are best classified pharmacologically as which of the following with respect to the H1 receptor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Competitive antagonists at the H1 receptor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Full agonists at the H1 receptor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Selective agonists at H2 and H3 receptors

explanation.summary: H1 antihistamines act by competitively binding to H1 receptors as antagonists or inverse agonists.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes H1 antihistamines as histamine antagonists and inverse agonists that work by competitively binding to H1 receptors, thereby blocking histamine's effects.

whyWrongByChoice.B: They oppose, rather than activate, the H1 receptor, so they are not full agonists.
whyWrongByChoice.C: They block the receptor; they do not inhibit histamine synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: They are receptor blockers, not enzymes that degrade histamine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: They target the H1 receptor and are not agonists at H2 or H3 receptors.

questions.topicName: H1 Blockers - Antihistamines

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man develops itching, hives, and nasal congestion minutes after exposure to pollen. The histamine responsible for his symptoms was released from which of the following cells?

explanation.summary: Histamine is stored in most body tissues but is found primarily in mast cells and basophils, which release it in response to allergens.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that histamine is stored in most body tissues and is primarily found in mast cells and basophils. Its release is often triggered by an allergen such as dust, pollen, or other irritants, producing itching, swelling, and inflammation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Gastric cells express H2 receptors that respond to histamine; they are not the primary storage site for histamine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Endothelial cells carry the H1 receptors that histamine and antihistamines act on; they do not release the histamine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bone marrow is where H4 receptors are located, not the main cellular store of histamine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Histamine acts on nerve endings to cause flare and itch, but sensory neurons are not its primary storage cells.

questions.topicName: H1 Blockers - Antihistamines

questions.stem: A pharmacology student reviews the physiologic roles of histamine beyond the immune response. In addition to mediating local immune responses and regulating gastrointestinal function, histamine acts as a neurotransmitter in which of the following sites?

explanation.summary: Histamine acts as a neurotransmitter in the brain, spinal cord, and uterus.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes histamine as mediating local immune responses throughout the body, regulating physiological functions in the gastrointestinal tract, and acting as a neurotransmitter in the brain, spinal cord, and uterus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The liver, pancreas, and kidney are not listed as sites where histamine serves as a neurotransmitter.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The heart, lungs, and adrenal medulla are not the neurotransmitter sites the brick names for histamine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Skeletal muscle, bone, and skin are not described as sites of histamine neurotransmission.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The thyroid, spleen, and bladder are not where histamine acts as a neurotransmitter.

questions.topicName: H1 Blockers - Antihistamines

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl with allergic rhinitis has a feeling of fullness in both ears and a productive-sounding cough during pollen season. Which action of histamine at H1 receptors best explains these ear and chest complaints?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Inhibition of nitric oxide release from endothelium

choices.label: E
choices.text: Suppression of wakefulness in the brain

explanation.summary: Histamine binding to H1 receptors causes hyper-secretion by glandular tissue, producing nasal, chest, or ear congestion.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that binding of histamine to widespread H1 receptors causes vasodilation, itching, and hyper-secretion by glandular tissue, leading to nasal, chest, or ear congestion. The ear fullness and chesty cough reflect this glandular hyper-secretion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Inhibiting nitric oxide release is what H1 antihistamines do, causing vasoconstriction; histamine itself causes vasodilation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gastric acid secretion is mediated by H2 receptors on gastric cells, not the H1 effects producing congestion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Muscarinic blockade is a property of first-generation antihistamines, not an action of histamine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Histamine acting at brain H1 receptors promotes wakefulness rather than suppressing it, and this would not cause congestion.

questions.topicName: H1 Blockers - Antihistamines

questions.stem: A neuroscience lecture describes the physiologic role of histamine acting at H1 receptors in the brain. When these central H1 receptors are activated by histamine, which of the following states is promoted?

explanation.summary: When activated, H1 receptors in the brain promote wakefulness, which is why blocking them causes drowsiness.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that when activated, H1 receptors in the brain promote wakefulness. First-generation antihistamines that cross the blood-brain barrier block these centrally located receptors and therefore cause drowsiness.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Sedation results from blocking, not activating, central H1 receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Nausea is not the state promoted by central H1 activation; antimuscarinic first-generation agents are in fact used to treat nausea.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Increased appetite is listed as an adverse effect of first-generation antihistamines, not the physiologic result of H1 activation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Motion sickness is a condition treated by antimuscarinic first-generation agents; it is not produced by central H1 activation.

questions.topicName: H1 Blockers - Antihistamines

questions.stem: A researcher is characterizing the tissue distribution of the four histamine receptor subtypes. The H4 receptor is found primarily in which of the following locations?

explanation.summary: H4 histamine receptors are located in the bone marrow.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists the receptor distribution as H1 widespread throughout the body, H2 primarily in gastric cells, H3 in the neurons, and H4 in the bone marrow.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gastric cells are the primary site of H2, not H4, receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Neurons are the site of H3 receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Vascular endothelium expresses the widespread H1 receptors targeted by antihistamines.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The uterus is a site where histamine acts as a neurotransmitter, but it is not the location the brick assigns to H4 receptors.

questions.topicName: H1 Blockers - Antihistamines

questions.stem: Figure 1 depicts an allergen binding to receptors on the surface of a mast cell, followed by release of histamine granules. Which intracellular change in the mast cell immediately precedes histamine release in this sequence?

explanation.summary: Allergen binding activates the mast cell and raises intracellular calcium, triggering histamine release.
explanation.whyCorrect: Figure 1 shows the allergen bound to the activated mast cell with a rise in intracellular Ca2+ (up-arrow Ca2+), after which histamine is released to act on H1 receptors of target cells such as smooth muscle, producing itching, swelling, and inflammation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A fall in potassium is not the mast cell signal shown; the figure indicates increased calcium.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Prostacyclin release is inhibited by H1 antihistamines acting on endothelial cells, not an event inside the mast cell before degranulation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nitric oxide release is affected downstream at the endothelium by antihistamines; it is not a mast cell trigger.
whyWrongByChoice.E: H1 receptor activation on the target cell occurs after histamine is released, not before it.

questions.topicName: H1 Blockers - Antihistamines

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman with chronic urticaria notes that after starting cetirizine, the red flare surrounding her wheals and the intense itching both diminish. Which action of the drug best explains reduction of the flare and itch?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increased nitric oxide release causing vasodilation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Suppression of histamine action on nerve endings

choices.label: C
choices.text: Blockade of H2 receptors on gastric cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inhibition of calcium entry into mast cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Antagonism of muscarinic receptors in skin

explanation.summary: H1 antihistamines suppress the action of histamine on nerve endings, reducing the flare and itch of endogenous histamine release.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that, in addition to producing vasoconstriction at the endothelium, H1 antihistamines suppress the action of histamine on nerve endings, which reduces the flare and itch associated with endogenous histamine release.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antihistamines inhibit, rather than increase, nitric oxide release; increased vasodilation would worsen the flare.
whyWrongByChoice.C: H2 receptors in gastric cells are unrelated to skin flare and itch, and cetirizine is an H1 agent.
whyWrongByChoice.D: H1 antihistamines act at the receptor on target cells; they do not block calcium entry or histamine release from mast cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cetirizine is a second-generation agent that acts on H1 receptors; muscarinic antagonism is not how flare and itch are reduced.

questions.topicName: H1 Blockers - Antihistamines

questions.stem: A pharmacist is sorting antihistamines into first-generation and second-generation bins. Which of the following belongs in the first-generation bin?

explanation.summary: Dimenhydrinate is a first-generation H1 antihistamine; loratadine, fexofenadine, desloratadine, and cetirizine are second-generation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists first-generation H1 antihistamines as diphenhydramine, chlorpheniramine, hydroxyzine, doxylamine, promethazine, and dimenhydrinate. Second-generation agents are loratadine, fexofenadine, desloratadine, and cetirizine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Desloratadine is a second-generation, non-sedating antihistamine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fexofenadine is a second-generation agent.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cetirizine is listed among the second-generation antihistamines.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Loratadine is a second-generation, non-sedating antihistamine.

questions.topicName: H1 Blockers - Antihistamines

questions.stem: A medical student compares diphenhydramine with loratadine. Which of the following is a property shared by both drugs?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lipophilic structure that readily crosses the blood-brain barrier

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antimuscarinic activity useful for motion sickness

choices.label: C
choices.text: Blockade of centrally located H1 receptors that promote wakefulness

choices.label: D
choices.text: Competitive binding to H1 receptors that inhibits nitric oxide release

choices.label: E
choices.text: Utility as a non-FDA approved sleep aid

explanation.summary: All H1 antihistamines, regardless of generation, competitively bind H1 receptors and inhibit nitric oxide and prostacyclin release; the generations differ mainly in central penetration and antimuscarinic activity.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the entire class acts by competitively binding to H1 receptors on cell surfaces, antagonizing endothelial H1 receptors to inhibit nitric oxide and prostacyclin release and produce vasoconstriction. The differences between generations are described as slight and relate to lipophilicity, blood-brain barrier penetration, and antimuscarinic properties.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Only diphenhydramine is lipophilic; loratadine is hydrophilic and penetrates the brain poorly.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antimuscarinic activity is a first-generation property; second-generation agents like loratadine lack it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Central H1 blockade, and the resulting drowsiness, is characteristic of first-generation agents only.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Use as a sleep aid depends on lipophilic first-generation agents crossing the blood-brain barrier; loratadine is non-sedating.

questions.topicName: H1 Blockers - Antihistamines

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man develops widespread hives, lip swelling, and wheezing after a bee sting and is treated in the emergency department. Alongside definitive management of his severe allergic reaction, an H1 antihistamine is added as an adjunct. Which agent is the brick's example for this role?

explanation.summary: First-generation antihistamines such as diphenhydramine serve as an adjunct treatment in severe allergies and anaphylaxis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Under clinical uses for allergies, the brick notes that first-generation antihistamines (e.g., diphenhydramine) are also an adjunct treatment in severe allergies/anaphylaxis, in addition to the vasoconstriction and reduced edema produced by H1 blockade.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Loratadine is a second-generation agent used for routine allergy symptoms; it is not the example given for anaphylaxis adjunct therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fexofenadine is a peripherally acting second-generation agent, not the adjunct named for severe allergic reactions.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Desloratadine is second-generation and is not cited as the anaphylaxis adjunct.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cetirizine is a second-generation antihistamine, not the first-generation adjunct the brick describes.

questions.topicName: H1 Blockers - Antihistamines

questions.stem: An 82-year-old woman who lives alone asks her physician for a first-generation antihistamine to treat seasonal allergies. Beyond the general risk of drowsiness, which specific complication does the brick emphasize as a reason for extra caution in this age group?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increased risk of falls and confusion

explanation.summary: In elderly patients the sedative effect of first-generation antihistamines can increase the risk of falls and confusion.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's clinical correlation advises extra caution when prescribing first-generation antihistamines to elderly people because the sedative effect can increase the risk of falls and confusion.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Paradoxical CNS stimulation is the concern in children younger than six years, not in the elderly.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reduced breast milk production is an antimuscarinic concern in lactating women, not in an 82-year-old.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gastric acid is regulated by H2 receptors; H1 antihistamines do not increase acid secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Birth defects are a pregnancy consideration, and the brick states antihistamines are unlikely to be strong risk factors for them.

questions.topicName: H1 Blockers - Antihistamines

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with nausea and vomiting after a viral illness is given chlorpheniramine, and his symptoms improve. The antiemetic benefit of this drug is most closely related to which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Its selective blockade of peripheral H1 receptors

choices.label: C
choices.text: Its blockade of H2 receptors in gastric cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Its hydrophilic nature limiting brain penetration

choices.label: E
choices.text: Its stimulation of nitric oxide release

explanation.summary: Promethazine and chlorpheniramine treat nausea and vomiting through their antimuscarinic activity.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that some first-generation antihistamines, namely promethazine and chlorpheniramine, are useful in treating nausea and/or vomiting, and that the mechanism is related to the antimuscarinic activity of these drugs. Figure 2 likewise lists decreased vomiting among the anticholinergic GI effects.
