whyWrongByChoice.A: Selective peripheral H1 blockade describes second-generation agents, which lack antiemetic antimuscarinic activity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: H2 blockade affects gastric acid secretion and is not the mechanism of chlorpheniramine's antiemetic effect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Chlorpheniramine is a lipophilic first-generation agent; a hydrophilic profile would describe second-generation drugs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: H1 antihistamines inhibit rather than stimulate nitric oxide release, and that vascular effect is unrelated to vomiting.

questions.topicName: H1 Blockers - Antihistamines

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman with occasional insomnia buys an over-the-counter product whose active ingredient is diphenhydramine and finds it helps her fall asleep. Which of the following best characterizes this use of the drug?

choices.label: A
choices.text: FDA-approved indication based on H2 receptor blockade

choices.label: B
choices.text: Non-FDA approved use based on peripheral H1 blockade

choices.label: C
choices.text: Non-FDA approved use based on central H1 blockade

choices.label: D
choices.text: FDA-approved indication based on antimuscarinic activity

choices.label: E
choices.text: FDA-approved indication based on histamine release

explanation.summary: First-generation antihistamines are sometimes used as non-FDA approved sleep aids because their lipophilic nature lets them cross the blood-brain barrier and cause drowsiness.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that the lipophilic nature of first-generation antihistamines allows them to easily cross the blood-brain barrier and block central H1 receptors that promote wakefulness, causing drowsiness. This effect is sometimes targeted to use them as non-FDA approved sleep aids.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Sleep-aid use is not FDA-approved, and diphenhydramine acts at H1, not H2, receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Peripheral H1 blockade does not produce sedation; it is central blockade that causes drowsiness.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The sedative effect stems from central H1 blockade rather than antimuscarinic activity, and the use is not FDA-approved.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Antihistamines block histamine's effects; they do not cause histamine release, and this use is not FDA-approved.

questions.topicName: H1 Blockers - Antihistamines

questions.stem: A 22-year-old college student plans to take hydroxyzine for itching before attending a party where alcohol will be served. Which of the following is the most important counseling point regarding this combination?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alcohol will block the antihistamine's binding to H1 receptors

choices.label: B
choices.text: The combination is likely to cause paradoxical CNS stimulation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Alcohol will convert the drug to a non-sedating agent

choices.label: D
choices.text: Drowsiness from the antihistamine will be more troublesome with alcohol

choices.label: E
choices.text: The combination increases gastric acid secretion

explanation.summary: Drowsiness from first-generation antihistamines is particularly troublesome when combined with other CNS depressants or alcohol.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that the unwanted drowsiness of first-generation antihistamines, which readily cross the blood-brain barrier, can be particularly troublesome if the patient is taking other concomitant CNS depressants or ingests alcohol. Hydroxyzine is a first-generation agent.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alcohol does not prevent H1 receptor binding; the concern is additive CNS depression.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Paradoxical CNS stimulation is described in children younger than six, not as a consequence of alcohol co-ingestion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Alcohol does not alter the lipophilic, sedating nature of hydroxyzine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Gastric acid secretion involves H2 receptors and is not the interaction the brick warns about.

questions.topicName: H1 Blockers - Antihistamines

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man taking a first-generation H1 antihistamine reports dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, and difficulty starting his urine stream. A student asks why blocking histamine would cause so many problems. Which of the following is the most accurate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: H1 receptor blockade in the periphery directly reduces gland and smooth muscle activity

choices.label: B
choices.text: These effects reflect blockade of H2 receptors in the gut and bladder

choices.label: C
choices.text: Second-generation agents produce identical effects at equivalent doses

choices.label: D
choices.text: These symptoms represent paradoxical stimulation of the CNS

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most adverse effects arise from muscarinic blockade rather than H1 blockade

explanation.summary: The majority of first-generation antihistamine adverse effects come from antimuscarinic activity; the antihistaminic action itself has comparatively few side effects.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that some first-generation H1 antihistamines have anticholinergic (anti-muscarinic) activity, that the majority of the adverse effects arise from this mechanism, and that the anti-histaminic receptor activity has comparatively few side effects. Dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, and urinary retention are the antimuscarinic effects summarized in Figure 2.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Peripheral H1 blockade produces vasoconstriction and reduced edema; it is not the source of these anticholinergic symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.B: H2 receptors are primarily in gastric cells and regulate acid, not bowel motility, salivation, vision, or urination.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Second-generation agents largely lack antimuscarinic activity and their side effects are mild and non-specific.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Paradoxical CNS stimulation manifests as restlessness and insomnia in young children, not as this peripheral anticholinergic picture.

questions.topicName: H1 Blockers - Antihistamines

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man works in his garden on a hot afternoon after taking diphenhydramine for hay fever. He notices that, unlike usual, his skin stays dry despite the heat. This finding is best explained by the drug's anticholinergic effect on which organ listed in Figure 2?

explanation.summary: Anticholinergic activity of first-generation antihistamines decreases sweating.
explanation.whyCorrect: Figure 2 summarizes the anticholinergic side effects of antihistamines by organ, listing decreased sweating as the effect on the skin. A lipophilic first-generation agent such as diphenhydramine has this antimuscarinic property.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Decreased salivary secretions cause dry mouth, not dry skin in the heat.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Decreased lacrimation produces dry eyes, a different organ effect from reduced sweating.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Decreased urination reflects bladder effects and does not account for absent sweating.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Decreased intestinal motility produces constipation, unrelated to sweating.

questions.topicName: H1 Blockers - Antihistamines

questions.stem: A student is asked to match each organ in Figure 2 to the effect produced by the anticholinergic activity of first-generation antihistamines. Which of the following organ-effect pairs is correct?

explanation.summary: Anticholinergic activity decreases urination (urinary retention), along with mydriasis, dry secretions, constipation, and decreased sweating.
explanation.whyCorrect: Figure 2 lists the anticholinergic effects as mydriasis and decreased lacrimation (eyes), decreased secretions/dryness (salivary glands), decreased GI secretions, decreased vomiting, and decreased intestinal motility/constipation (GI), decreased urination (urinary bladder), and decreased sweating (skin).

whyWrongByChoice.A: The ocular effect is mydriasis (dilation), not miosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Salivary secretions are decreased, causing dryness, not increased.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Intestinal motility is decreased, producing constipation, not increased.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sweating is decreased, not increased.

questions.topicName: H1 Blockers - Antihistamines

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman who is exclusively breastfeeding her 2-month-old infant takes chlorpheniramine for several days for allergy symptoms and notices her milk supply has dropped. Which property of the drug best explains this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Its inhibition of nitric oxide release

choices.label: D
choices.text: Its inability to cross into breast tissue

explanation.summary: The antimuscarinic properties of many first-generation H1 antihistamines can reduce breast milk production in lactating women.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that, due to the antimuscarinic properties of many first-generation H1 antihistamines, they can reduce breast milk production in the lactating woman. Chlorpheniramine is a first-generation agent.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Inhibition of nitric oxide release produces vasoconstriction that relieves congestion; it is not linked to milk production.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chlorpheniramine blocks H1, not H2, receptors, and H2 blockade is not the cause of reduced milk.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The drug's distribution into breast tissue is not the mechanism; its antimuscarinic action reduces production.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Paradoxical CNS stimulation is a pediatric phenomenon and does not affect lactation.

questions.topicName: H1 Blockers - Antihistamines

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman at 20 weeks' gestation took diphenhydramine for several nights for hives before realizing she was pregnant and is now worried it harmed her fetus. Which of the following is the most accurate counseling statement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The drug does not cross the placenta, so the fetus was never exposed

choices.label: B
choices.text: The drug is a known strong risk factor for major birth defects

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only second-generation antihistamines cross the placenta

choices.label: D
choices.text: The drug crosses the placenta but is unlikely to be a strong risk factor for major birth defects

choices.label: E
choices.text: Exposure is expected to cause paradoxical CNS stimulation in the fetus

explanation.summary: H1 antihistamines readily cross the placenta but are unlikely to be strong risk factors for major birth defects.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states in two places that H1 antihistamines cross the placenta but are unlikely to be strong risk factors for major birth defects; indeed, doxylamine with pyridoxine is approved for nausea and vomiting of pregnancy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick explicitly says H1 antihistamines readily cross the placenta.
whyWrongByChoice.B: They are described as unlikely to be strong risk factors for major birth defects.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Placental crossing is described for H1 antihistamines generally, and the pregnancy discussion centers on first-generation doxylamine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Paradoxical CNS stimulation is described in children under six taking the drug, not as a fetal effect.

questions.topicName: H1 Blockers - Antihistamines

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman taking a first-generation antihistamine for chronic pruritus is reviewed for adverse effects. Of the following effects the brick attributes to H1 antihistamines, which is described as rare?

explanation.summary: Among the adverse effects of H1 antihistamines, psychosis is specifically noted to be rare.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists undesirable effects including incoordination, anxiety, blurred vision, increased appetite, vomiting, constipation, diarrhea, dry mouth, urinary retention, delirium, hallucinations, and psychosis, adding that the latter (psychosis) is rare.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dry mouth is a common antimuscarinic effect and is the answer to the brick's own review question on common side effects.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Blurred vision is a typical anticholinergic effect, not singled out as rare.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Constipation from decreased intestinal motility is a standard anticholinergic effect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Drowsiness is the most common effect of first-generation agents, not a rare one.

questions.topicName: H1 Blockers - Antihistamines

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman has taken hydroxyzine nightly for several months for itching and has gained weight. She also reports clumsiness and anxiety. Which additional finding would be most consistent with a recognized adverse effect of this drug class?

explanation.summary: Increased appetite, incoordination, and anxiety are among the listed adverse effects of first-generation H1 antihistamines.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's list of undesirable side effects of H1 antihistamines includes incoordination, anxiety, blurred vision, increased appetite, vomiting, constipation, diarrhea, dry mouth, urinary retention, delirium, hallucinations, and psychosis. Increased appetite fits her weight gain, and her clumsiness and anxiety match incoordination and anxiety.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Anticholinergic activity causes urinary retention (decreased urination), not polyuria.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Salivary secretions are decreased, producing dry mouth rather than excessive salivation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The ocular effect is mydriasis (dilated pupils), not pinpoint pupils.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sweating is decreased by anticholinergic activity, so profuse sweating is not expected.

questions.topicName: H1 Blockers - Antihistamines

questions.stem: Four patients request an antihistamine. For which of the following patients is a first-generation agent the more appropriate choice over a second-generation agent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A 4-year-old boy with seasonal sneezing whose parents want him calm at bedtime

choices.label: B
choices.text: A 36-year-old man who becomes nauseated on long boat trips

choices.label: C
choices.text: An 80-year-old woman with hay fever who has fallen twice this year

choices.label: D
choices.text: A 33-year-old woman with hives who is breastfeeding a newborn

choices.label: E
choices.text: A 41-year-old airline pilot with itchy eyes during flights

explanation.summary: First-generation agents are preferred when their antimuscarinic activity is therapeutic, as in motion sickness, but should be avoided when sedation or antimuscarinic effects are hazardous.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that first-generation antihistamines such as promethazine and dimenhydrinate have antimuscarinic properties effective in treating motion sickness, an action second-generation agents lack. Each other patient has a stated reason for caution with first-generation drugs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Children younger than six can experience paradoxical CNS stimulation with restlessness and insomnia from first-generation agents.
whyWrongByChoice.C: In the elderly, the sedative effect increases the risk of falls and confusion, so a non-sedating agent is preferred.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antimuscarinic properties of first-generation agents can reduce breast milk production in a lactating woman.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A pilot needs to remain alert; a non-sedating second-generation agent is the appropriate choice.

questions.topicName: H1 Blockers - Antihistamines

questions.stem: In the brick's sorting exercise, drugs must be placed into first-generation and second-generation bottles. Which of the following groups contains only second-generation antihistamines?

explanation.summary: The second-generation H1 antihistamines are loratadine, fexofenadine, desloratadine, and cetirizine.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists the second-generation, non-sedating H1 antihistamines as loratadine, fexofenadine, desloratadine, and cetirizine. All other agents in the sorting exercise (diphenhydramine, chlorpheniramine, hydroxyzine, doxylamine, promethazine, dimenhydrinate) are first-generation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hydroxyzine is a first-generation antihistamine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Doxylamine is first-generation; it is the agent paired with pyridoxine for nausea of pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Promethazine is a first-generation agent used for motion sickness and nausea.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Chlorpheniramine is a first-generation antihistamine.

questions.topicName: H1 Blockers - Antihistamines

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man is stung by a wasp and within minutes develops a red, swollen, intensely itchy welt at the site. The receptor subtype mediating the vasodilation and itching of this local response is best described as which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: H2 receptors located primarily in gastric cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: H4 receptors located in the bone marrow

choices.label: D
choices.text: H1 receptors widespread throughout the body

explanation.summary: Histamine binding to widespread H1 receptors causes vasodilation, itching, and glandular hyper-secretion, which is why H1 receptors are the target of antihistamine therapy.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that H1 receptors are widespread throughout the body and that binding of histamine to these receptors causes vasodilation, itching, and hyper-secretion by glandular tissue. Figure 1 shows histamine acting on the H1 receptor of a target cell to produce itching, swelling, and inflammation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: H2 receptors in gastric cells regulate acid secretion, not the vasodilation and itch of a local sting reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: H3 receptors are in neurons and are not the mediators of the cutaneous flare and itch described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: H4 receptors in bone marrow are not responsible for the local skin response.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Muscarinic receptors are blocked by first-generation antihistamines as a side effect; they do not mediate histamine's itch and vasodilation.
